requirement_title: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly
requirement_text:
# REQ-2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129
Type: feature

## Requirement

Given Project A (contains `ProjectA.MyType`, has no and cannot have a reference to the MessagePack NuGet package) and Project B (references Project A and MessagePack), the reporter needs a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for `ProjectA.MyType` generated inside Project B.

Proposed solution: add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that works for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

The class does not need a body; the implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

For attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), the issue lists three alternatives: (1) use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes; (2) let the generator and analyzers work with user-defined copies of the MessagePack attributes; (3) source-generate the attributes themselves via `RegisterPostInitializationOutput`.

Motivation: Project A is a NuGet library that should stay minimal with zero dependencies.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute exists and can be applied to a partial class implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.
- The source generator emits the formatter implementation for `T` inside the annotated class, in the assembly that declares the class (Project B), even when `T` is declared in a referenced assembly.
- The annotated class may be declared without a body (`partial class X : IMessagePackFormatter<T>;`).
- `T` needs no MessagePack attributes: without `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` on `T` the generated formatter uses contractless behaviour over public members. (derived from maintainer comment)
- If `T` does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Private members are not required to be serialized; only public members are in scope. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Project A needs no reference to the MessagePack package. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- AArnott: "We might simplistically say this only works in 'contractless' mode, such that you need no attributes on it at all. If there are attributes on it, fine, we'll use them. But if there is no `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` attribute on the type, go contractless by default."
- AArnott on prerequisite: "Does ProjectA.MyType requires only `public` members to be serialized? That seems a prerequisite for anything here." Reporter: yes.
- AArnott is not a fan of a `PropertyKeys` dictionary on the formatter, and warns that copying attributes into Project A breaks reflection-based (dynamic resolver) mode.
- AArnott suggested a surrogate-type design: `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter(SurrogateType = typeof(ProjectASurrogate))]`, keys mapped by property name; reporter: "Looks good." No design was settled in the thread.

product-context: deliberate per ledger, not a defect: Requirement says a type in a referenced assembly gets a formatter generated in the consuming assembly; the ledger entry says TypeCollector deliberately skips metadata-only types. The new GeneratedFormatterCollector bypasses that path and is explicit opt-in, so there is no conflict. The absence of an automatic formatter for external types remains deliberate.
Receipts/GeneratedFormatterReferencedAssemblyTests.cs: requirement test fails on base (2/2), passes on head (2/2)
Receipts/GeneratedFormatterHonoursAttributesTests.cs: edge-case test passes on head (2 tests): no defect shown; refutes 1 lens claim(s): requirement-tests-1
Receipts/GeneratedFormatterAndTimestampReceipts.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 4/4 failed

Mutation: 11 killed, 5 survived, 3 compile errors, 0 timeouts (19 mutants on MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.cs, GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs, ObjectSerializationInfo.cs, GeneratorUtilities.cs, MessagePackGenerator.cs, MessagePackPrimitives.Writers.cs)
Compatibility bytes: 4/124 cases differ, 0 base payloads fail to read on head, public API +3/-0

findings.claim: This hunk is unrelated to the requirement and corrupts timestamp data. The timestamp32 branch now tests `(data64 & 0x00000000ffffffffL) == 0` instead of the upper 32 bits. Values whose low 32 seconds bits are zero (e.g. the Unix epoch plus non-zero nanoseconds, or seconds = 2^32) are written as a 4-byte timestamp32, which drops the nanoseconds and the high seconds bits. Every ordinary whole-second DateTime that used to encode as timestamp32 now encodes as timestamp64, changing the wire bytes.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime values with base-built and head-built MessagePack and compare the bytes: `new DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc)` gives d6 ff (6 bytes) on base and d7 ff on head. Then round-trip `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` on head: the deserialized value loses its nanoseconds, so it is not equal to the input.

findings.claim: The contractless member set excludes public get-only properties and readonly fields, and constructor parameters are never matched. The existing contractless behaviour (ContractlessStandardResolver, L3) serializes public readable members and populates them via a matching constructor. So a T with get-only properties, or with only a parameterized constructor, is either silently not serialized or rejected. The requirement asks for "contractless behaviour over public members".

receipt_plan.detail: Define a referenced type `public class P { public P(int id){Id=id;} public int Id { get; } }`. Serialize it with ContractlessStandardResolver and with the generated formatter, and compare: the dynamic resolver writes {"Id":..}, while the generated formatter is rejected (MsgPack007/no ctor) or would write an empty map.

findings.claim: The timestamp32 guard was inverted. The new code takes the 4-byte timestamp32 path when the LOW 32 bits of data64 are zero, but timestamp32 is only valid when the HIGH 32 bits (the nanoseconds plus the upper seconds bits) are zero. Example: DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1) gives seconds=0, nanos=100, so data64=100<<34 and its low 32 bits are zero. It is written as timestamp32 with payload (uint)data64 == 0, the nanoseconds are lost, and the value reads back as the exact epoch (silent data corruption). The same happens at every multiple of 2^32 seconds with a non-zero fraction. In addition, every whole-second date such as 2020-01-01 now takes 10 bytes instead of 6, so the wire bytes change from base.

receipt_plan.detail: Run GeneratedFormatterAndTimestampReceipts.DateTime_EpochPlusOneTick_RoundTrips: serialize DateTime(1970-01-01 UTC).AddTicks(1) with MessagePackSerializer and deserialize; the ticks differ on head. Run GeneratedFormatterAndTimestampReceipts.DateTime_WholeSecond_UsesTimestamp32: 2020-01-01 UTC serializes to 6 bytes on base and 10 on head.

findings.claim: Contractless mode ignores every MessagePack attribute on the formatted type T. CreateContractlessMembers takes all public read-write members, sorts them by name and uses string keys, never looking at [MessagePackObject], [Key] or [IgnoreMember] on T. Example: a T from a referenced assembly with [MessagePackObject], [Key(0)] Value and [IgnoreMember] Secret. The generated formatter still serializes Secret and writes a string-keyed map instead of an int-keyed array. The acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured' is not met. The resulting wire format also differs from the one the dynamic resolver produces for the same type.

receipt_plan.detail: Run GeneratedFormatterAndTimestampReceipts.AttributedReferencedType_IgnoreMemberIsHonoured and AttributedReferencedType_IntKeysProduceArray. Each emits a ProjectA assembly whose MyObject carries [MessagePackObject]/[Key(0)]/[IgnoreMember], runs MessagePackGenerator on a ProjectB with [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class MyObjectFormatter, and inspects the generated formatter text.

findings.claim: The mask in the timestamp writer was changed from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. The timestamp32 branch is now chosen when the low 32 bits are zero. That is wrong: it should apply when the high 32 bits (nanoseconds) are zero. Timestamps with zero nanoseconds and nonzero seconds now take the 64-bit path, and values with a zero low 32 bits may take the 32-bit path and lose data. This changes the serialized bytes of DateTime and DateTimeOffset values for every user, and it is unrelated to the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize new DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc) with MessagePackSerializer and the native DateTime formatter on base and head builds, and compare the bytes. Base emits the 6-byte timestamp32 form (0xd6 0xff ...). Head emits the 10-byte timestamp64 form (0xd7 0xff ...). Also run a round trip for a value whose seconds are a multiple of 2^32 with nonzero nanoseconds.

findings.claim: Contractless members are sorted ordinally by name and read-only members are dropped. Standard contractless serialization keeps declaration order and includes members that are readable but not writable, such as constructor-initialized members. Wire output from the generated formatter differs from ContractlessStandardResolver for the same type. A consumer in Project B who mixes the dynamic and generated formatters would see different map key order. The requirement says only 'contractless behaviour over public members'.

receipt_plan.detail: For a type with public properties Z and A declared in that order, serialize with ContractlessStandardResolver and with the generated formatter, then compare the bytes. Key order should differ.

findings.claim: The change modifies the shared runtime MessagePackPrimitives.Writers.cs timestamp encoding (mask 0xffffffff00000000 changed to 0x00000000ffffffff), which is unrelated to REQ-2129. It inverts the timestamp32 vs timestamp64 selection, so values that fit in 32 bits would now use the 64-bit format and vice versa, corrupting or changing wire bytes. The ledger notes numeric serialization is bug-prone.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime values such as 1970-01-01T00:00:01Z (timestamp32) and one with nonzero nanoseconds using base-built and head-built MessagePack, then compare bytes; also run the existing timestamp tests.

findings.claim: Unrelated change to the timestamp writer condition (0xffffffff00000000 -> 0x00000000ffffffff) has no test in the diff. Mutation here would corrupt DateTime/timestamp encoding: timestamp32 would be chosen only when the low 32 bits are zero, so ordinary timestamps would take another path. No test in the diff exercises timestamp encoding.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime/Timestamp (e.g. 2020-01-01 UTC, nanoseconds=0) with base-built and head-built MessagePack; compare bytes. Expected: base emits 6-byte timestamp32 (0xd6 0xff), head emits 10-byte timestamp64.

hunches.claim: The timestamp writer mask was inverted from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. The timestamp32 branch is now chosen when the low 32 bits of data64 are zero, not when the high 32 bits are zero. Timestamps with zero nanoseconds and nonzero seconds (e.g. data64 = seconds) have non-zero low bits, so they fall through to timestamp64. Timestamps whose low 32 bits happen to be zero are written as timestamp32 with the data truncated, which corrupts the value. Data written is wrong and round-trips lose information.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize DateTime/DateTimeOffset values such as 1970-01-01T00:00:01Z, 2020-01-01Z, and one with nonzero nanoseconds, via MessagePackPrimitives.TryWriteTimestamp. Deserialize and assert equality. Also byte-diff base vs head to show format changes (0xd6 vs 0xd7) and value truncation.

hunches.claim: Contractless member ordering and key assignment (OrderBy name, intKey: i) has no test that detects a change. The tests only check string keys via JSON Contains and a header byte 0x82; a mutant removing OrderBy or altering the ordering would survive.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs:157 delete-statement: .OrderBy(m => m.Name, StringComparer.Ordinal) -> removed; expected to survive because tests assert only Contains on JSON and round-trip, not byte order.

hunches.claim: Surrogate string-key mode is never tested end to end (only integer-key surrogate in execution tests), so the `intKey: members.Count, stringKey: (string)key` branch and the string-key detection are unverified. Duplicate-key (KeysMustBeUnique), MemberNeedsKey, and no-parameterless-constructor (NoDeserializingConstructor) paths also have no tests.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs:215 remove-guard: `if (!claimedKeys.Add(key))` -> `if (false)`; expected to survive because no test has a surrogate with duplicate keys.

hunches.claim: The GeneratedFormatterMustImplementFormatter test only covers zero interfaces; the `Length != 1` case with multiple IMessagePackFormatter<T> interfaces is untested. The Collect-side check for inaccessible/generic/struct data types is likewise untested (only abstract). No generator snapshot (regeneration) test covers the new partial-class template output.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs:61 negate-condition: `formatterInterfaces.Length != 1` -> `== 0`; expected to survive because no test implements two formatter interfaces.

hunches.claim: The GeneratorUtilities filter that excludes [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] classes from hand-written formatter registration is only indirectly tested; a duplicate registration might not be noticed by GeneratedFormattersAreRegisteredInGeneratedResolver, which only checks the returned type.

receipt_plan.detail: GeneratorUtilities.cs:38 remove-guard: delete `!symbol.GetAttributes().Any(...)`; expected to survive because tests only assert resolver returns the right type.

hunches.claim: IsPartial checks only the formatter's own declaration. The template re-emits the formatter inside its nesting types via EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces. A formatter nested in a non-partial containing class (class Outer { [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class F : IMessagePackFormatter<X> {} }) would therefore produce generated code that redeclares Outer, giving CS0260/CS0101, with no MsgPack019 diagnostic explaining why.

receipt_plan.detail: IsPartial (GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs, bottom of file) inspects only formatter.DeclaringSyntaxReferences. Containing types are never checked, while FormatterTemplate.tt wraps the output in EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces.

hunches.claim: The user-declared formatter template emits `partial class Name` with no accessibility modifier or `sealed`. Generated output for ordinary formatters is unchanged, but the diagnostic registration only lists the new ids. The new descriptors MsgPack019-022 are not shown in AnalyzerReleases.Unshipped.md, and the analyzer's SupportedDiagnostics lists them, so RS2000 release-tracking errors may appear. Docs for the help links are also missing.

receipt_plan.detail: Check that AnalyzerReleases.Unshipped.md has rows for MsgPack019-022 and that doc/analyzers/MsgPack019-022.md exist.

hunches.claim: Generated formatters in surrogate or contractless mode skip the analyzers' protections. Diagnostics are produced through a separate collector pass with the real `Collect` call passing reportDiagnostic: null. Rejected formatters (non-partial, no parameterless ctor) silently produce nothing in the model path; this is mitigated by the diagnostic pass. The model path drops errors with no failure, so security-relevant analyzer rules (e.g. MsgPack003/004 equivalents) are not applied to the referenced type. This is a minor concern only; the diagnostics pass exists.

receipt_plan.detail: Read MessagePackGenerator.cs: the model pass calls Collect with reportDiagnostic: null while the diagnostic pass calls it again with diagnostics.Add. Verify both give consistent results via a generator snapshot test with an invalid formatter.

hunches.claim: New diagnostics MsgPack019-022 are added to the docs and AnalyzerReleases.Unshipped.md, but the analyzer only registers descriptors. The partial, formatter-interface and data-type diagnostics are reported from the generator via RegisterSourceOutput. The first-listed generator-reported diagnostics will not appear in the IDE as live analyzer results, and a surrogate-less formatter gets no diagnostic if the analyzer never runs on it. This is a mismatch between the documented analyzer behavior and the actual implementation.

receipt_plan.detail: Compare the registration in MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.Initialize with the diagnostics reported by MessagePackGenerator.generatedFormatterDiagnostics.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Contractless over public read-write members, with an optional SurrogateType to define keys. The type's own MessagePack attributes are not read. Constructor-less types are rejected.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: The collector also reads [MessagePackObject]/[Key]/[DataContract] attributes on T when present, using them for keys, ignore and unions. It falls back to contractless only when no attributes exist, and the surrogate is not needed.
